Mood Regulation

Spontaneous and Pharmacologically Assisted

Mortimer Ostow MD

Mortimer Ostow

4421 Douglas Avenue, Riverdale, New York 10471, U.S.A.
email: MOstow1234@aol.com

Mortimer Ostow   Read at the International Psychoanalytic Congress, Santiago, Chile, 1999.

Mood is a constant affective background to all of conscious life. It fluctuates between pleasurable and energizing on the one hand, and depressive and enervating on the other. Mood responds to incident environmental influences and to internal, instinctual influences, but it also exhibits rhythmic fluctuations that influence behavior. Mood dysregulation creates affect disease, and the therapeutic agents that one uses to treat affect disease do so by controlling mood. Psychopharmacologic experience helps us to understand the principles of mood regulation and its effect on normal and abnormal behavior. Mood controls psychodynamics rather than vice versa. Important social issues such as apocalypticism and fundamentalism are ultimately mood driven. Mood is a significant psychic parameter that correlates with the many neuroscientific processes that are coming to light.

Freud's Theory of Mind and Functional Imaging Experiments

Robert Shulman and Morton Reiser MD

Morton Reiser

MR Center, P.O. Box 208043, New Haven, CT 06520-8043, U.S.A.
email: robert.shulman@ yale.edu

New Haven, Connecticut, U.S.A.

Morton Reiser  

13C in vivo NMR experiments have measured large neuronal neurotransmitter fluxes in resting rat and human brains which are coupled to brain energy consumption. In the awake, resting state this “baseline” neuronal activity accounts for ∼80% of brain energy consumption. The resting activity decreases with deepening anesthesia. In stimulated anesthetized rats, high localized somatosensory brain activity is restored by incremental changes during forepaw stimulation. Functional imaging experiments generally measure such incremental changes in activities during a task period and discard the highly active baseline. Single electrode measurements of the spiking rates in a representative population of neurons in the rat somatosensory region have been correlated with the functional imaging under the same stimulation. The population response has allowed patterns from the sensory stimulation to be distinguished from connections with the brain's global activity. In this way it is becoming possible to identify global task activities that include the organismic responses normally submerged in the large unassigned baseline activities. We propose that the high baseline plus any incremental activity supports total mental activity across all levels of mentation. In contrast to cognitive psychology, which neglects baseline and assumes that task activities are supported by measurable increments, we suggest that Freud's layers of consciousness provide a more fitting conceptual framework for understanding brain activity and its relation to mentation. Freud's topographical model of mind is consistent with the high neuronal activity that is required to support tasks, and its layered structure offers an interpretive guide to total brain activities.

Commentary on “The Pleasantness of False Beliefs”

Marcel Kinsbourne MD

Marcel Kinsbourne

Marcel Kinsbourne   New School University, New York, U.S.A.

Confabulation: A Psychic Wonderland?

“Will you, won't you, will you, won't you, will you join the dance?”

Lewis Caroll, Alice's Adventures in Wonderland

The question

Brain damage may drive mental life either outward or inward, to join or not to join the Dance. In the latter case, it may unveil an underlying level of mental function that previously was covert. With that possibility in mind for the genesis of confabulations, Turnbull, Jenkins, and Rowley present an innovative study of the emotional valence of confabulations uttered by three patients with ventromesial frontal injury. They nest their empirical presentation in a more extensive discussion of method and theory.

Confabulation has been defined as “spontaneous narrative reports of events that never happened” (Schacter, Norman, & Koutstaal, 1998). This definition has to be qualified by the fact that the event may be in the present or future, as well as in the past (for a recent and comprehensive review, see Schnider, 2003). Whether the patients really believe what they are saying or are instead speaking metaphorically is hard to ascertain, and not part of the definition. However, the patients are not merely misinformed, and conscious attempts to deceive are also excluded from the construct.

Confabulation is associated with organic amnesia, prefrontal deficits, or both in conjunction (DeLuca, 2000). In some cases, it reflects flawed emergence of language at the level of which concepts are specified in that domain (Brown, 1988). In others, there is flawed emergence of meaning. Confabulatory speech has been attributed to failure of the brain to monitor the emerging proposition for accuracy (Johnson, 1997). These and others models of confabulation do not take into consideration the expected valence of confabulatory utterances. Turnbull and coauthors conceive the issue from a psychoanalytic perspective, as lapsed editing of primary-process contents by secondary processes, before they are expressed in words (Solms, 2000). They therefore bring the question of emotional valence into the discussion. If confabulation is a disinhibited expression of a covert underlying mental state—specifically, primary process—one would expect it to express or symbolize the emotional valence of that state as well as its ideational content. I have previously suggested that confabulation is fostered by “an inner-directed focus on an affectively laden issue, a focus that is so intense and narrow that it excludes peripheral information, or memories that might conflict with the favored interpretation of the situation” (Kinsbourne, 2000a, p. 159).

Affect Regulation and Loss of Initiative in a Case of Orbitofrontal Injury

Birgit Mathiesen , Pernille Vedel Förster and Henriette Svendsen

Henriette Svendsen

Njalsgade 90, DK-2300 Copenhagen S, Denmark
(email: birgit.bork.mathiesen@psy.ku.dk).

Henriette Svendsen   Henriette Aaby Svendsen: Department of Psychology, University of Copenhagen, Copenhagen, Denmark.

Personality change after injury to the orbitofrontal cortex has frequently been described in the literature. However, there are only a few specific and reliable methods available for the assessment of personality change after brain injury. Here we present a patient, LP, whose personality has changed due to a ruptured aneurysm of the anterior communicating artery that resulted in bilateral ventromesial prefrontal lesions. Although his performance on extensive conventional neuropsychological tests was within normal range, he exhibited severe behavioral problems characterized by lack of initiative, inappropriate social timing, and blunt affect. The patient's behavioral problems were measured with extensive assessment of personality characteristics and traits using methods from psychodynamic and psychometric traditions. Although no general signs of psychopathology were found, there were some indications that he was suffering from personal problems that fluctuated, as cognitive functions sometimes do after frontal-lobe injury. Intensive psychoanalytic psychotherapy allows us to hypothesize about some of the dynamics behind his acquired “loss of initiative,” although the very nature of his problems appears to be an obstacle to this kind of psychotherapy. This case study, like similar ones presented in the literature, reminds us to be cautious of accepting negative findings concerning standardized test performance as evidence of the absence of real-life problems after frontal-lobe injury.

Douglas Watt  

This is a rich, dense, and poetic book about big problems and big ideas—the self, consciousness, and qualitative elements of experience (qualia). Neuroscience has made vast progress by putting these problems to one side and addressing more tractable questions. Yet these big problems continue to stand out, as they have since people started contemplating the relationship of mind and brain. Inattention to them has particularly disrupted the relationship between the neurosciences and disciplines like psychoanalysis that center on personal experience.

One source of psychoanalysts' reluctance to incorporate neuroscience in their studies is the sense that there is an irreducible essence of a person's being that cannot be imagined to result from physical events. The problem of selves—or should we say, souls—haunts the interface of neuroscience and psychoanalysis. Despite attempts to address the problem and, even, convincing arguments that it is a pseudo-problem, analysts commonly worry that neuroscientists ignore what is most important to people about their psychological lives—the subjective experiences of consciousness and self.

In psychoanalysis, the self is conceptually slippery. Difficulties start with Freud's loose equation of mental content involving one's person with the idea (translated into English as ego) of a coherent set of functions that mediate between drives, superego, and the external world and include consciousness. Despite efforts to disentangle self and ego, the ideas remained entwined, partly because disturbed ego function and problematic self-experience often co-occur. Heinz Kohut, the most influential psychoanalytic thinker on the self, avoided definitions, stating that it is an “experience-near concept”—that is, something everyone knows from personal experience. Satisfactory self experiences, Kohut observed, include coherence over time and space and a sense of vigor.

Among psychological motives, maintaining a satisfactory sense of self is most important, comparable to a drowning person's press for oxygen.

Decision-Making, Empathy, and Reward

Eisenberger, N. I., Lieberman, M. D., & Williams, K. D. (2003). Does rejection hurt? An fMRI study of social exclusion.Science, 302: 290-292.

This interesting study investigates the neurobiological basis of social exclusion, which might also be regarded as “loss” or the pain of separation. It involved a functional- imaging investigation of scanned brains of subjects playing “virtual” catch with two others. The participants believed that the images of other characters represented the real players—though the task was run by computer program. The players initially believed that they were part of a group throwing a ball between themselves. However, in an “explicit-rejection” condition, the other (imaginary) players deliberately ignore the participants— rejecting them as they passed the ball between themselves. Unsurprisingly, participants showed feelings of exclusion, measured by self-report, in the “rejection” condition. Critically, activity in the anterior cingulate cortex—an area long known to be associated with feelings of separation and loss—was increased during this condition. The authors also note that this brain area has previously been linked to the experience of physical pain, hence the analogy that “pain” of the social type might be analogous to physical pain. In addition, activity in the right ventral prefrontal cortex was correlated with reduced distress after the rejection. The authors note too that this area has previously been linked with the regulation of (physical) pain. The study is yet another suggesting a role for the anterior cingulate cortex in the attachment process, adding an additional role for the frontal cortex in affect regulation.

Bar-On, R., Tranel, D., Denberg, N. L., & Bechara, A. (2003). Exploring the neurological substrate of emotional and social intelligence.Brain, 126: 1790-1800.

Neurological patients with lesions to the ventromesial frontal lobes have long been described as having normal intelligence, and they often have normal or near- normal performance on a range of “executive” tasks (e.g., Bechara, Damasio, Damasio, & Anderson, 1994; Damasio, 1996). However, in spite of such apparently normal performances, they often choose unsuitable friends, enter inappropriate relationships, and engage in ill-advised activities—leading to financial losses, career termination, and loss of affection of family and friends. There are good grounds for considering that such poor judgment and decision-making skills follow from an inability to use emotion-learning systems, which provide information about the outcome of decisions and their possible emotional consequences (Damasio, 1996). This role for emotion in cognition, sometimes referred to as emotion-based learning, also resembles other attempts at defining the role of affective phenomena in decision making—such as the concept of “emotional intelligence” (Lane & Schwartz, 1987). This literature has suggested that awareness of the nature of emotional experience is likely to be a key factor in using emotion-related knowledge to guide decision making—a phenomenon that we subjectively experience as “intuition.” In this paper, Bar- On et al. investigate a group of patients with neurological lesions on measures of “emotional intelligence” and also on established measures of emotion-based learning (the Iowa Gambling Task). Patients with lesions in the ventromesial frontal lobes, and in other brain regions associated with emotion-based learning (such as the amygdala), performed poorly on both the emotional intelligence and the emotion-based learning tasks yet showed normal intelligence. A control group was normal on both measures. There is much work to be done on identifying precisely what is meant by concepts such as “emotional intelligence,” but studies such as this suggest that the concept seems to have validity and suggests links to a range of neurobiological substrates involved in emotion.

Yoram Yovell  

This issue's Target Article, by Robert Shulman and Morton Reiser, is an investigation and reconsideration of research using functional imaging, and offering a link to psychoanalysis. The paper focuses especially on the question of how we might interpret the levels of baseline activity in the brain, in contrast to the incremental activity associated with specific reactions to perceptual events. As usual, the article is followed by a set of commentaries by neuroscientists and psychoanalysts, who discuss the technical details of the proposal as well as their relationship to broader theoretical questions.

In the Original Articles section we publish an empirical investigation by Claudio Colace on the dreams of addicts, as well as a historical investigation by Malcolm Macmillan considering possible links between Freud and the classic neurological case, Phineas Gage. The Ongoing Discussion section contains several responses to an article written by Mortimer Ostow in the 2004:1 issue of Neuro-Psychoanalysis.

We have also taken this opportunity, in a new section entitled Founders of Neuro-Psychoanalysis, to publish the first in what we hope will be an ongoing series of interviews with senior members of our field. Appropriately, the interview in this issue is with Dr. Ostow. The interview series aims to discuss with senior figures why they chose to work on the neuroscience/psychoanalysis boundary in an earlier era, when such an interest was deeply unfashionable. There is special focus on the many ways in which the field has changed since their initial interest, seeking also their opinion on why the field has flourished in recent years, as well as their comments on what they see as the longer-term future of neuro-psychoanalysis. We welcome suggestions from readers of the journal about which individuals might be suitable to be interviewed in the series.

As always, the issue concludes with the Book Review, Research Digest, and International Bulletin sections.

Finally, we announce that the annual Arnold Z. Pfeffer Prize for 2003 has been awarded to Jaak Panksepp, for his seminal work in the area of Affective Neuroscience, most notably on the anatomical and pharmacochemical basis of emotional consciousness.

Mortimer Ostow   New York, U.S.A.

I am indebted to my colleagues for seriously considering my essay, encouraging me where they agree, and showing me problems where they disagree. Perhaps the distinction I make between affect and mood should be sharpened, or at least I should observe the distinction more consistently. In the essay I dodged defining affect since its meaning to my readers is well known, if not always given precisely. I subscribe to Panksepp's proposition that consciousness probably exists in all mammals and possibly in less-evolved creatures, and that its ultimate function is to perceive and record affect. “Affect is a neurodynamic quality of consciousness—a quality that is quite indescribable verbally but has dimensional attributes such as valence, arousal, and surgency,” Panksepp and Pincus write, and they remind us of the appraisal function of affect.

While not all affective experience is generated as a component of an instinctual process, many of the more intense affects that intrude into our consciousness are. And for these I have provided an original taxonomy based upon the position of that type of affect in the structure of the instinctual process. As my discussants note, I did not fail to allow for affects that are not immediately associated with, or derive from, instincts. Neubauer refers to these as “based on external influence from the ego apparatus.

The Textbook of Biological Psychiatry is aimed at a number of related disciplines who occupy their professional work at what Jaak Panksepp calls “the middle level of analysis where mental faculties can be related credibly to objective brain systems in ways which may be clinically productive” (p. 27). The book gives clinicians the information needed to perform state-of-the-art treatment, and at the same time it presents a conceptual framework with which to evaluate research that will be coming through our journals over the next period. Dr. Panksepp's diplomatic and yet innovative stance pervades a work that represents many schools of thought and perspectives on both psychiatric disorders and clinical treatments.

The textbook is divided into three sections, “Foundational Concepts,” “Core Psychiatric Challenges,” and “Future Prospects.” In the first section, the reader is oriented in the most sophisticated way to basic ways of thinking about psychiatry, in which Dr. Panksepp gives his history of the field in the twentieth century. In the second chapter, he begins a discussion, cowritten with Mario Liotto, of radiological brain imaging and affective neuroscience. State and channel functions are a key idea here—that is, discrete informational/cognitive thinking can flow through distinct brain circuits—categorized and discussed by imaging changes in brain blood flow during an fMRI study. In contrast, moods are generated in a brainstem/limbic fashion. Drs. Panksepp and Liotto have an elegant illustration that shows the initiation and maintenance of an emotional state by switching off cortical regions, resulting in brainstem/limbic dominance—a structural/functional diagram of how we “lose it.” As I know from repeated experience, at times of intense emotional upheaval I cannot think straight. Dr. Panksepp presents cogent explanatory neuroscience concepts that underlie this very common human experience.

Dr. Panksepp has suggested a number of concepts that are major potential innovations in neuropsychiatric thinking. The foremost of these is his synthesis of decades of rat research to create his seven “basic emotional systems,” which are then discussed. Dr. Panksepp has been able to delineate many of the neural pathways and neurotransmitters involved in the SEEKING, RAGE, FEAR, PANIC, PLAY, LUST, and CARE systems. These are distinct although presumably interrelated systems; one or another may be dominant at any particular time, determined by the interaction of the animal and the environment, with the SEEKING system in a sense as foundational for the potential activation of all the other discrete systems—massive lesions of the SEEKING system create akinetic mutism (AKM) and wipe out all emotion and affective arousal. Underlining the critical importance of emotion for all motivated behavior, this syndrome of midbrain AKM (discussed by Watt & Pincus in some detail in Chap. 3) shows the wipe-out of any spontaneous behavior and a very poor prognosis.

The group is characterized by its informal nature (an open group) and heterogeneous membership, which has proved to be both a difficulty and an advantage. After a period of high turnover, we are now a group of 24 participants who are highly committed to our monthly meetings. We come from a wide range of professions: about two-thirds are mental-health professionals and art therapists, while the rest are clinical neurologists and neuropsychologists. Our main goal is trying to establish a working dictionary, in order to bridge the gap between the various participants of the group. After having studied the concept of “agency”—as described in our earlier report—we now aim at examining the different terms related to “control mechanisms” (monitoring, error detection, impulse control, ego functions, self-monitoring of social organizations, etc.).

During the spring of 2004, a series of cases were each presented by a clinician and discussed by another member, representing the neurobiological point of view. During these meetings we had fruitful discussions. We therefore wish to use this method as a model for our future meetings, and perhaps it is also a good format for eventually publishing our proceedings. With this in mind, we devoted two meetings to obsessive compulsive disorder (OCD), with two discussants: a neuropsychologist and a psychoanalyst. The discussion centered around similarities and differences between the psychoanalytic literature concerning OCD and the underlying neuropathology of the disorder.

We have also discussed issues of pain as it is processed somatically and experienced emotionally, its monitoring functions, and its emotional valence. With the help of a neurologist and a movement therapist, we addressed the problem of motor control by studying the awareness of Chorea patients of their abnormal movements.

We end each meeting with 15 minutes of reflection on the work done during the meeting. This procedure involves the group in reflecting on the way in which we learn and how it contributes to our experience. Planned meetings now include emotional and neuropsychological aspects of music, and monitoring functions in borderline personality disorder. We hope to publish our work in the form of short monographs (e.g., on control mechanisms), but we are still looking for a publisher.

Oliver Turnbull  

Many a Foolish Notion: Emotion and Confabulation

My thanks, first, to the commentators for taking the time and effort to respond.

Empiricism and quantification

The question of empiricism and quantification ran through the commentaries as a common, and generally positive, theme. Almost all the commentators appeared to welcome the fact that evidence generated in a psychoanalytic context should be tackled in a manner that suggested a desire to measure phenomena in a tractable manner, and with a reasonable level of experimental control. There was, of course, some disagreement about the specifics of how this was achieved (e.g., Blechner, DeLuca, Schnider, and others). For example, several commentators raised, quite rightly, matters related to sampling and control in the study: why this series of patients, and which criteria were employed in selecting them; why were the patients not worked up in greater detail in terms of their performance in conventional neuropsychological assessment, and their everyday behavior not documented in greater detail; why were there not more appropriate control groups?

Answers to these questions follow, in large part, from an understanding of the nature and purpose of the study. The study was conducted post hoc, as a reinvestigation of previously studied cases. Our goal was not to investigate confabulations in the manner expected of an entirely conventional neuropsychological study. This would have required a more systematic neuropsychological work-up of the patient, a betterdesigned method for ensuring that all possible confabulations were evaluated, and the addition of a control group. Such a study would also be submitted for publication in a conventional neuropsychological publication—as we have now done (e.g., Fotopoulou, Solms, & Turnbull, 2004; Turnbull, Berry, & Evans, 2004). These studies have addressed basically the same question as that in the study under consideration here, and they produced a more or less identical conclusion of possible emotional bias in confabulation.

It is not surprising that Ostow—a pioneer investigator of the correlation between psychopharmacological and psychoanalytic investigation—offers us, in his paper, condensed data and far-reaching findings. Featured Article

Farah, M. J., Illes, J., Cook-Deegan, R., Gardner, H., Kandel, E., King, P., Parens, E., Sahakian, B., & Wolpe, P. R. (2004). Neurocognitive enhancement: What can we do and what should we do?Nature Reviews Neuroscience, 5: 421-425.

The question of ethical issues in neuroscience was reviewed in the 2003:1 issue of the Research Digest. In this more recent article, Martha Farah has encouraged a number of prominent figures in the fields of modern neuroscience and ethics (readers will recognize, for example, Eric Kandel on the author list) to band together and outline a general position on one aspect of this important topic. The central theme is that this century will show a growing ability to directly modify brain function, producing changes that “might well shape history as powerfully as the development of metallurgy in the Iron Age, mechanization in the Industrial Revolution or genetics in the second half of the twentieth century” (p.421). These advances in “neurotechnology” will be implemented through a wide range of techniques, from the well-known example of psychopharmacology, through transcranial magnetic stimulation, to the implantation of stimulation devices, tissue transplants, and even the possibility of brain-machine “interfaces”—a technology that has already shown remarkable promise. These innovations will be manifest in a number of important ways— not only in the ethically “simple” case of treating mental illness, but also in the ability to enhance the mental capabilities of “normal” individuals. It is this topic of neurocognitive enhancement that is the focus of the Farah et al. discussion paper. The possibility of “enhancement” raises issues on several counts: for example, what might be safe, including striking a balance between anticipated outcome and side-effects. Also, there is the question of what might be “fair,” given that there is likely to be unequal access to these resources. Health services are unlikely to pay for your attentional capacities or executive abilities to be enhanced, yet many medically normal university students in the United States (the paper cites a top-range figure of 16%) are finding study-related benefits associated with metheylphenidate (Ritalin). There are similar pharmacological possibilities for enhancing otherwise “normal” memory function—or, indeed, for taking a pharmacological agent that will allow you to forget an unpleasant experience you may have just had (i.e., a proactive treatment for potential PTSD)! Finally, there is the larger question of whether such enhancement is morally acceptable, linked to the question of whether the genie can ever be kept in the bottle.

Commentary

Jack Gorman MD

Jack Gorman

Jack Gorman   Esther and Joseph Klingenstein Professor and Chair, Department of Psychiatry, Mount Sinai School of Medicine, New York, U.S.A.

In the past two decades, much has happened in the relationship between psychoanalysis and psychophar-macology. Originally, the so-called pharmacological revolution in psychiatry that began in the late 1950s was seen as a direct challenge to psychoanalytic theory and practice. Trainees through the 1960s and 1970s were often faced with the demand to choose sides: psychopathology is either the result of unresolved unconscious conflict or abnormalities in the levels of neurotransmitters. The latter point of view even denigrated the importance of dreams. A prominent scientist at the time held that dreams represented responses to random changes in serotonergic neuronal firing and therefore carried no coherent meaning of use to the mental health professional.

Although, to be sure, there are some who still indulge in these dichotomies, they seem woefully old-fashioned nowadays. We no longer believe that the level of a particular neurotransmitter has much to do with an illness like depression or panic disorder. Rather, modern neuroscience has begun to show us that emotional regulation involves the coordinated function of brain circuits that involve multiple chemical messengers. Furthermore, the intensity of response of these circuits in any individual is dependent on inherited factors and experiential shaping. Freud said essentially the same thing on multiple occasions, beginning as early as the “Project” (1895). Neuroscientists today speak comfortably about the “unconscious,” although they are most likely to refer to it as “implicit” memory, and to acknowledge that early life experience has profound influence on the emotional nature and behavior of organisms for the rest of their lives.

Mortimer Ostow, in retrospect, seems to have known this all along. It is hard to think of a psychoanalyst who did more to champion the benefits of psy-chopharmacology. But most importantly, Ostow has done this without sacrificing his allegiance to the legitimacy of psychoanalytic theory. For him, medications do not replace dream interpretation; the two go hand in hand. The present article is a wonderful case in point.

This commentary—kindly invited by the Editors of Neuro-Psychoanalysis—considers an article published therein by Vesa Talvitie and Juhani Ihanus, bearing the title “On the Nature of Repressed Contents—A Working-Through of John Searle's Critique.”1 I was probably asked to submit the present commentary mainly because, nearly a decade ago, a publication of mine on the same topic appeared. Published in Consciousness and Cognition, that article (Natsoulas, 1995) was critical of John R. Searle's (1992) account of Sigmund Freud's conception of consciousness and the relation of consciousness to those mental occurrences that Freud held to be unconscious. My critique of Searle's account was a sequel to an article, “A Rediscovery of Consciousness,” in which I treated of certain aspects of his mental philosophy (Natsoulas, 1994).

Another determinant of the decision to ask me to write this commentary may have been my unified series of articles on Freud's theory of consciousness that, for close to two decades, have been appearing in the journal Psychoanalysis and Contemporary Thought (e.g., Natsoulas, 1984a, 1985, 1991, 1993a, 2002a, 2002b, 2003). Add the fact that, between Talvitie and Ihanus and myself, there is much overlap in scientific interests—even if one judges only on the basis of their article for which the present response was sought. However, I do not want to imply that I agree with (a) all of Talvitie and Ihanus's statements about the theories of Freud and Searle, (b) their proposed “logic” of the repressed psychical processes, (c) their proposed computer metaphor for the psychical apparatus, or (d) their scientific philosophy of eliminativism—according to which scientific progress benefits from the restriction of theories and concepts to those acceptable to a favored scientific and philosophical contingent.

In all of my writings and lectures on Freud's understanding of consciousness, I have followed him and his editor/translator in consistently using the term psychical process to make reference to the mental-occurrence kind that Freud focused on. Readers will recall that Freud distinguished three kinds of psychical process: the conscious, the preconscious, or merely descriptively unconscious, and the repressed, or dynamically unconscious.

Commentary on “Freud's Theory of Mind and Functional Imaging Experiments”

P. Matthews MD D.Phil. F.R.C.P.

P. Matthews

Oxford, U.K.

P. Matthews  

Perhaps the greatest problem facing neuroscience is to understand how phenomena of mind can emerge from activity in the brain. Current cognitive neuroscience, the study of brain systems for cognition, most frequently has adopted network-based computational models when making direct relations between mind and brain. Such models involve processing nodes (ideally physically localizable) interacting in specific patterns within a functional network.

The popularity of computational network models has been motivated in part by the success of hierarchical and modular theories of brain mechanisms, as is best illustrated by the visual system. Here, sensory afferent information is processed serially by distinctly localized subcortical and cortical systems that define features ultimately “bound” together into a specific percept. This model is hierarchical in that perception develops from a partially sequential progression of information-processing steps. The model is modular as it includes distinct processing elements that add definable characteristics to perceptual experience, such as color or motion.

Such models have provided both an explanation for neurological deficits with brain lesions and predictions of possible types of deficits. The hierarchical nature is consistent with the lack of any visual experience with damage to the primary visual cortex, for example.

Commentary on “Freud's Theory of Mind and Functional Imaging Experiments”

Robert Turner PHD

Robert Turner

London, U.K.

Robert Turner  

Ever since it was recognized, more than 50 years ago, that the human brain expends roughly 20% of our total energy intake, even when we are deeply asleep, the question has arisen: what does it do with all that energy? More recently, the question has become more sharply defined as neuroimaging techniques have been perfected. Radiotracer methods (PET and single photon emission computerized tomography—SPECT) for observing local cerebral changes in metabolism and blood flow were the first to be used, by the mid-1980s. These were followed, and largely superseded, a decade later by the advent of functional MRI, which offered the huge advantage of being entirely noninvasive, using only the effects on the signal from water protons of the endogenous tracer, deoxyhemoglobin, to track changes in blood flow that correlate with changes in brain energy use.

The ability to visualize task-related changes easily by means of sensitized images of the brains of normal volunteers has naturally stimulated renewed reflection regarding the nature of mind and its relationship to the physical brain. One uncontroversial way of describing the relationship is to say that “the mind is what the brain does”—what we choose to call “mind” being the physiological processes taking place in brain tissue. However, this does not greatly alleviate the problem of relating the often very useful terminology, developed over many years, for describing mental processes and events to that describing brain processes and events. Some writers, such as Dennett, seek to demystify and deconstruct mentalistic terminology but tend to fall into the self-contradictory traps endemic to positivism. Others, simplistically, believe that all mental states can be explained in physicalist terms, and they invoke models for brain function analogous to computers. It is such writers that are the targets of the present strongly worded polemic. Shulman and Reiser accuse the cognitive science community at large of taking little or no account of the intense baseline activity of the brain, as if such activity were no more than “noise,” and conceiving of the brain as a “logic machine.

Commentary on “The Pleasantness of False Beliefs”

Armin Schnider MD

Armin Schnider

Armin Schnider   Médecin-chef de service, Service de Rééducation, Département des Neurosciences Cliniques, Hôpitaux Universitaires de Genève, Geneva, Switzerland.

Being a neurologist working in a rehabilitation clinic and regularly seeing patients who fail to adapt their thinking to ongoing reality, I considered it an extraordinary honor to be invited to comment on the article by Turnbull, Jenkins, and Rowley. But when I read the article, I realized that it has an entirely different approach from my own studies. It starts with an astonishing introduction—confabulations are portrayed as if they represented one homogeneous disorder, with unknown mechanism, and a diffuse anatomical basis! The introduction lumps together extremely broad classes of speculations about confabulations that I thought had been convincingly disproved (“processes related to executive function”). I am quoted within the group of seeming defenders of an executive hypothesis, which we have disproved in a number of studies: neither the severity of amnesia nor the severity of executive failures explains the occurrence of or the recovery from diverse forms of confabulations (Schnider, 2000; Schnider & Ptak, 1999; Schnider, Ptak, von Däniken, & Remonda, 2000; Schnider, von Däniken, & Gutbrod, 1996a). The hypothesis of the study revives, albeit under a new title, the century-old idea that confabulations reflect a desire (wish) to fill gaps in memory (Bonhoeffer, 1904; Pick, 1905). Studies testing this hypothesis found that, in comparison with other brain-damaged subjects, confabulators do not have an increased tendency to fill gaps in memory—that is, to respond to whatever question (Mercer, Wapner, Gardner, & Benson, 1977; Schnider, von Däniken, & Gutbrod., 1996a).

Clinicians have long made a distinction between provoked and spontaneous confabulations, without a clear idea about the pathophysiological and anatomical bases (Pick, 1905). In our observation of memoryimpaired patients, we soon realized that some amnesic patients' tendency to invent items when recalling a word list (provoked confabulations) was completely independent of and doubly dissociated from the tendency to spontaneously produce seemingly invented stories to justify behaviors that were incompatible with current reality (spontaneous confabulation) (Schnider, von Däniken, & Gutbrod, 1996a). The latter patients typically act on the basis of memories that may have justly guided their behavior in the past but are inadequate guides for present behavior. For example, a dentist with rupture of an anterior communicating artery aneurysm repeatedly left the hospital in the conviction that he had to see patients at his clinic (see also Ptak & Schnider, 1999; Schnider, 2003; Schnider, von Däniken, & Gutbrod, 1996a). The syndrome of spontaneous confabulation reflects a failure to refer thinking and behavior to ongoing reality; the confabulations are just the verbal expression of this failure.

More than three years ago, we initiated a series of courses with the aim of spreading neurobiological insights into the functioning of the mind, as well as the observable changes related to the implementation of various therapies. We were also interested in developing a training milieu in which the contributions of neuroscience could be discussed, so as to understand the fundamentals of psychoanalysis as well as the contributions of psychoanalysis in guiding new potential developments within the neurosciences.

We have addressed neuro-psychoanalysis with a special emphasis on the fact that our objective is not reductionistic in regard to psychoanalysis. On the contrary, we are convinced that there is a possibility of an integrated coevolution for both sciences. In support of this “coevolutive” view, we have taken recourse to modern concepts that stem from another recent integrationist approach—namely, that of neurophilosophy.

In August 2000 we started a course on basic neurobiology (especially for residents of psychiatry and psychology), which, due to public demand, was extended to include neurophysiopathology and neuroimaging.

During 2003 the development of this project resulted in three courses:

Psychoanalysis and neuroscience—a nonreductionistic approach.

The neurobiology of subjectivity, affect, and sexuality.

The neurobiology of mental disorders

For two years we have given a distance-teaching course on neurobiology, in Spanish, making use of the efficient ways of presenting the material offered by the internet. During 2004 we hope to be able to publish a book on neuroscience “tailored” especially for psychologists and psychiatrists.

It would be of great interest for our institution to establish closer links to the International Society of Neuro-Psychoanalysis so as to exchange experiences and enhance the development of the important and interesting field of neuro-psychoanalysis.

James Deutsch

James Deutsch  

The Toronto group is now in its third year. It consists of interested professionals from a number of disciplines and backgrounds, having in common a commitment to continued inquiry into the links between psychoanalysis and neuroscience. Difficult clinical cases, with or without clear neurological syndromes, form a focus of discussion, following presentations. The group has shown particular interest in traumatic and depressive syndromes.

Dr. James Deutsch reviewed the 4th International Neuro-Psychoanalysis Congress (“The Unconscious in Cognitive Neuroscience and Psychoanalysis,” July, 2003, New York City) in two sessions. From the vast amount of material, it was chosen to focus on two general approaches to unconscious mental functioning. Dr. Solms' presentation on confabulatory syndromes exemplifying the characteristics of primary process was based on patients who had tragically suffered from brain damage resulting in interference with memory function. Together with the approach of Drs. Shevrin and Brakel, and colleagues, using subliminal (less than 1-msec) stimulation or probing of the mode of categorization of figures, it is apparent that careful neuroscientific study confirms key characteristics of primary-process functioning, a key observation in Freud's early studies of unconscious mentation.

In the group's discussion, cases involving psychological trauma, with or without neurological damage, challenged us in our own attempts to categorize levels of mental functioning. The helpful descriptions and categories of Dowling (1982), along with those of Piaget (1973), affirmed the importance of careful, psychoanalytically informed observation of process in assessment and treatment. In severe psychological trauma, it would appear that there is a “pre-primary process functioning,” which, in metapsychological terms, involves the relatively inactivated ego and is outside the pleasure principle.

Diverging perhaps somewhat from the focus of the International Congress, there was discussion and speculation on the contribution of the interaction of the hippocampus and amygdala to the formation and retrieval of memories. The ideas of Layton and Krikorian (2002) about a continuum based on relative activities of hippocampus and amygdala, ranging from “flashbulb memories” to posttraumatic phenomena, were applied to case narratives brought by members of the group. There is interest in correlating the relative contributions of these brain structures to the generation and maintenance of preprimary-process (sensorimotor), primary-process, and secondary-process functioning.

Commentary on “The Pleasantness of False Beliefs”

Todd Feinberg MD

Todd Feinberg

Todd Feinberg   Division Chief, Yarmon Neurobehavior and Alzheimer's Disease Center, Beth Israel Medical Center, New York, U.S.A.

Before I address the specifics of the interesting paper by Turnbull, Jenkins, and Rowley, I would like to review some literature on the issue of the role of motivational and emotional factors in confabulation and anosognosia. In 1944, Paterson and Zangwill described confabulatory patients in a posttraumatic confusional state that misidentified their current location to a geographical location closer to their actual home. Paterson and Zangwill also noted that during the course of recovery, the patients would maintain that they were simultaneously located in both the correct and the incorrect locations, a condition that Pick (1903) called reduplicative paramnesia. Paterson and Zangwill observed that these patients were oblivious to the conflict presented by their dual orientation and would confabulate explanations when confronted with the disparity. These patients might accept the correct orientation in an “abstract geographical” sense, such as knowing the correct locale “according to the map”, but still maintain that they “felt” they were located closer to home.

Paterson and Zangwill made two important observations regarding this disorientation: (1) while amnesia was initially present, the “retention deficit cleared rapidly” and memory was adequate to recall the day's events a full week before correct orientation returned, and (2) some patients with this disorder verbally expressed a strong desire to return home. These features led Paterson and Zangwill to conclude that affective and motivational factors played a significant role in persistent disorientation. They suggested that under the conditions of brain damage, motivational factors were “actively inhibiting the cognitive mechanisms which normally subserve orientation,” and this accounted for the persistent disorientation when “cognitive recovery had proceeded far enough to permit and sustain proper orientation.” They interpreted the disorientation on the basis of both the negative features— in a Jacksonian sense (Taylor, 1958)—of anterograde and retrograde amnesia, restriction of perception, and a defect in judgment in which there is a failure to correct incompatible interpretations, as well as the positive features of affect and motivation.

Diego Cohen

Diego Cohen

email: diegocohen@fibertel.com.ar

Diego Cohen  

“Freud's Model of Dreams and the Neurobiology of Sexuality”

Under my coordination, the Psychoanalysis and Neuroscience Chapter of the APA began meeting in August 2003, with the aim of studying the fundamentals of neuroscience and the bases for major concepts in psychoanalysis and their clinical applications. In the first stage, we have touched upon the origins of psychoanalysis and neuroscience through Freud's works on aphasia and the “Project” (1895), with the intention of correlating certain concepts of the “Project” with contemporary neuroscientific thinking.

The chapter has monthly meetings and is open to both members and nonmembers of the APA alike. During the spring of 2004, we have been working on the subject of dreams with the object of determining whether it is possible to find a correlation between the Freudian dream model (Freud, 1900) as a wish fulfilment (with its origin in early infancy and containing sexually repressed material) and the properties of the neurobiological system, which, hypothetically, we consider to be the neurobiological mediator in the search for situations of sexual pleasure.

Freud's contribution, through the study of dreams and of science in general, highlights that dreams make sense and introduces the interpretative-hermeneutic method, thus producing an important epistemological modification. For the fulfilment of desires, a central axis is given in their origin in infancy and containing previously repressed sexual desires.

We have studied the SEEKING system (SS) described by Panksepp (1998), a system that acts as mediator in brain-mind interactions, as in the case of dreams with childhood sexual content. The group arrived at the following conclusions:

“Dreams are the fulfillment of desires.”

“Dreams are the fulfillment of desires that appear disguised.”

“Dreams are the disguised fulfillment of repressed desires.”

“Dreams are the disguised fulfillment of repressed childhood sexual desires.”

Panksepp's SS has the following main characteristics:

It is a neuroemotional circuit that uses dopamine (DA) as neurotransmitter (NT), and it intervenes in states of exploration/investigation/curiosity/interest.

“New Psychosomatic Horizons”

On 19 June 2004, the French group arranged its annual conference day, where members can present their research work. The main topic this year dealt with a new method of observing and diagnosing somatic patients, presented by Professor Jean Benjamin Stora. He described a “psychosomatic classification” model, where psychic, neuronal, and somatic functioning are integrated and where the domestic, social, and occupational environments of the patient are also included. The method is structured according to a “psychosomatic” grid composed of five axes. The grid has not only facilitated individual diagnosis but can also be used in epidemiologic researches. It was developed during the last 20 years but is not yet statistically verified. Jean Benjamin Stora has used it in studies on cancer and heart-transplant patients. It is seen as important to estimate the severity of the symptoms and thus attain a risk profile. This approach is radically different from the DSM-IV approach, because it implements psychoanalytic and psychosomatic concepts and relates to the human psyche as structured according to Sigmund Freud's two “topiques.”

Irene Epelbaum, clinical neuropsychologist, gave a talk on depression and the neurodegenerative diseases of old people. If the problem of dementia in elderly patients attracts all the attention, then depression in the old might be overlooked and underestimated. Demented states represent 20-40% of cases, and depression 40-60%. Neurodegenerative diseases can, of course, worsen depression.

The Body-Mind Study Groups of the Swedish Psychoanalytic Society

Iré Matthis , Magnus Kihlbom , Daniela Prawitz and Lennart Bryngelson

Lennart Bryngelson

email: magnus.kihlbom@swipnet.se

email: daniela.prawitz@psykolog.net

email: lennart@bryngelson.se

Lennart Bryngelson  

The body-mind theme is at the center of the activities of several study groups of the Swedish Psychoanalytical Society. The first group, initiated by Magnus Kihlbom and chaired by Iréne Matthis, started as early as the autumn of 1997. During the following years it spawned many offspring, related to different lines of interest. The first aim was to gain a deeper knowledge and enlarge the psychoanalytic perspective on the body-mind theme with the assistance of other disciplines, such as philosophy, semiotics, neuropsychology, psychosomatic medicine, and neuroscience. We are now trying to create a common ground (conceptually and clinically) for neuroscience and psychoanalysis for the exchange of experiences and ideas.

Over the years, more than 60 people have taken part in the work, some as members of several groups, others of only one. In May 2004, a joint meeting was organized for all present and former participants of the groups. Many responded to the invitation, and during a very successful and stimulating meeting, one person from each group reported on his or her group's activities during the last year. The meeting confirmed the value of this kind of seminar and the importance of the theme. Many expressed the wish to engage in discussions with others in the Society and from other disciplines.

International Society of Neuro-Psychoanalysis, Toronto Chapter

James Deutsch

James Deutsch

email: j.deutsch@utoronto.ca

James Deutsch  

During the spring of 2004, Eduard Bercovici, of the University of Toronto Epilepsy Research Program, gave a presentation on “Stress, Trauma, Depression, and Limbic System Processes.” Bercovici discussed various ways that stress can be defined and viewed, based on Sapolsky's (2003) article, “Taming Stress.” Stress disturbs homeostasis, causes excitability and arousal, involves lack of control of the situation, and is generally aversive. If stress is to leave a lasting impression on the organism, it must be converted from sensory information, through short-term memory and consolidation, into long-term memory. The hippocampus subserves the formation of declarative, explicit, autobiographical memories, while other structures, including cerebellum, amygdala, and hypothalamus, subserve nondeclarative/implicit memory. The relative sizes of the structures reflect the actualities of the particular research animal's life. Much memory research has been done on the rat (as it is nonspeaking, its chief mode of communication is through activity or behavior, which can be influenced by a number of factors having nothing to do with memory), which has limited applicability to studies on declarative memory.

Papez combined a number of structures into an emotional circuit. Stress activates this circuit. The hippocampus, involving reverberating circuits, is ideally suited to memory consolidation and the formation of links. The neocortex serves as substrate for distributed storage of memory. Long-term potentiation involves the formation of synaptic connections of increased efficiency; long-term depression, the necessary reverse of the process, enables the organism to adapt to the circumstances of a changing reality. This process can be illustrated by pathways in the snow: some become well used, but eventually the entire area becomes trampled, and the whole process loses meaning and significance—and, in the brain, could result in seizures—unless the process can somehow be reversed, with the restoration of untrodden areas. Pathways involving amygdala subserve quick, instinctive responses. Two parallel but interacting stress pathways involve the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis (corticotropin releasing hormone and glucocorticoids) on the one hand, and the locus coeruleus (norepinephrine) on the other. Explicit/declarative memory can be enhanced by acute stress but impaired by excessive stress. Excessive stress has opposite effects on hippocampus and amygdala. In the hippocampus, it reduces synaptic formation, alters morphology, decreases number of dendrites, and affects neurotransmitters. In the amygdala, the effects are generally the opposite. There may be a shift toward or away from explicit, declarative memory formation as a result. Stress also appears to have an effect on neurogenesis, or the formation of new nerve cells.

Yusaka Soussumi  

On 20-22 May 2004, CEINPSP organized a major event in São Paulo: “First Journey of Neuroscience and Psychoanalysis: A Meeting with Mark Solms.” The meeting was also supported by the Brazilian Society of Psychoanalysis in São Paulo, by the Institute “Sedes Sapientiae,” by the Brazilian Association of Psychiatry, and by the Institute of Research and Education in Medicine, Psychoanalysis, and Psychotherapy. The event was met with great interest by the scientific community in São Paulo, and it was completely sold out. On the first day, an extra room with a television screen had to be arranged to accommodate the audience.

Contact with the press

While in São Paulo, Dr. Solms was interviewed by Folha de S. Paulo, one of the two leading daily newspapers in Brazil. The interview was published in a Sunday issue, on 20 June. At the same occasion, Dr. Solms also gave an interview to Scientific American/Brazil.

In June, Dr. Soussumi and his collaborators were interviewed by the weekly magazine, Carta Capital, about their views on violence, seen from a neuro-psycho-analytic perspective. The interview was published in July 2004.

NGO

Aware of our country's social problems and the issue of violence, CEINPSP is at the present time involved in the organization of a nongovernmental institution named RUHKA. Its goal is to develop social activities for children in need and for adolescents. This involves creating and developing instruments that might help in the development of cognitive-emotional and moral self-regulation, socialization, and humanization and including, for example, video games and other computational devices that could be used and tested by the population in question. Economical investments will also be made by RHUKA in hiring professionals and establishing partnerships with universities and hospitals, for the purpose of conducting neuro-psychoanalytic research.

At the moment we are in the first phase of the project, which has as its main goal the development of a specific psychoeducational gadget with a videogame format. The full details will be ready and made public at the end of the second semester of 2004.

Confabulation Pleasant and Unpleasant

Turnbull, Jenkins, and Rowley present a study of the complex and fascinating neuropsychological phenomenon of spontaneous confabulation. In empirically revisiting the clinical material of Kaplan-Solms and Solms (2000), and by applying established neuroscientific methodologies, they produce findings that have genuine interdisciplinary merit. Their study falls within a newly developed and neuro-psychoanalytically informed approach that empirically accounts for emotional biases in confabulation (Fotopoulou, Solms, & Turnbull, 2004; Turnbull, Berry, & Evans, 2004). Such an approach provides an alternative motivational explanation to the various, predominantly cognitive, models of the phenomenon.

Jaak Panksepp and David Pincus

David Pincus

David Pincus   Case Western Reserve University, Cleveland Heights, Cleveland, Ohio, U.S.A.

Toward a Taxonomy of Affects

Ostow has given us a much-needed beginning toward a taxonomy of affects, which should eventually translate well from neuroanatomy and neurodynamics to psychiatry and psychodynamics. We are in dire need of the systematic study of affect from a variety of conceptual and practical viewpoints. We are not well served by the systematic neglect of affect in the neurosci-entific literature, or by its poor-cousin status in psychoanalytic literature and its truncation into static phenomenological categories in DSM-IV (APA, 1994). We are in full support of Ostow's initiative to find new directions in this enterprise and are reminded of Bion's (1970) suggestion that feelings are the few things that analysts have the luxury of being able to regard as facts. It is a great deficiency that nothing close to that can yet be said in the neurosciences, though there is a shift in the wind and emotion studies are currently among the hottest topics in integrative human brain research. Unfortunately, the subjective experience of emotions—the various affective states—is rarely monitored or discussed in such studies. Most analyses focus on cognitive, behavioral, and physiological issues that can be more easily objectified.

The triangle of emotional controls consists typically of (1) primary appraisal functions (sometimes as simple as evolutionarily primed sensory input like sounds that startle or smells that scare) that commonly instigate (2) arousal of various limbic processes that control instinctual emotional responses (behavioral, affective experiential, and physiological), which lead to (3) a large variety of secondary appraisal processes, both short-and long-term, related to cognitive coping with the affective states mediated by the limbic arousal. This last function, which is often the focus of cognitive approaches to emotions, may well reflect Freud's concept of “the taming of the affects” that occurs with ego and superego maturation. No one really knows how each of these general aspects of brain functioning contributes to affective experience, but ever since Paul MacLean popularized the concept of the limbic system in 1952, some of us in neuro-science have been willing to attribute much of the power of affect to those deep subcortical recesses of the mammalian brain. The “limbic” concept gave us, for the first time, a reasonable place within the brain to search for the detailed mechanisms of emotional behaviors and thereby, hopefully, for the sources of affective feelings (i.e., the valenced experiential aspects) that accompany emotional states (which in our terminology is the “umbrella” term that includes, beside affective, also the behavioral, cognitive, and physiological aspects). Unfortunately, there are forces afoot in neuroscience to deconstruct and demolish the limbic system concept (see discussions in Cory & Gardner, 2002), which we see as a premature, poorly focused, and hence ill-advised attempt to replace productive holistic ideas with more psychologically sterile micro-mechanistic puzzles (Panksepp, 2002, 2003).

Dr. Mortimer Ostow is a neurologist, psychiatrist, and psychoanalyst, who began wondering about the neural bases of psychodynamic processes while he was still a candidate in training at the New York Psychoanalytic Institute—an extremely brave stance to take at that time. His first publications on the topic date back to the early 1950s. He also made some perceptive observations on the psychodynamics of epilepsy and autoscopic phenomena, among other clinical neurological conditions. He then embraced the psychopharmacological revolution— observing the mental effects of the psychoactive drugs he began to use in his clinical practice, and again considering the probable metapsychological correlates of these powerful chemical agents. His seminal book on that topic, dating from the 1960s, remains a classic to this day. Dr Ostow has also had a life-long interest in the psychology of spiritual belief and mystical experience. He has played a major role in developing the field of neuro-psychoanalysis, including at the institutional level in recent years. Our field owes him a substantial debt.

This interview with Dr. Mortimer Ostow took place at the Hotel Wales, New York City, on 9 November 2002.

The similarities between the theories of thinking as inhibited action developed by David Ferrier and Sigmund Freud are examined in the context of the changes in the behavior of Phineas Gage, which Ferrier tried to explain with his inhibitory-motor theory. Johannes Müller's concept of will, its development by Alexander Bain, and Bain's influence on Ferrier's conceptualization of inhibitory centers localized in the frontal lobes are traced. Elements of the Bain-Ferrier theory found in Freud's theory of thinking, which do not derive from Brücke, Meynert, or Jackson, are itemized, and the implications of Freud's opting for a mechanism of inhibition that was basically excitatory is examined. Possible reasons for Ferrier's abandoning his concept of inhibitory centers are discussed and are contrasted with the reasons that Freud had for keeping to an excitatory conceptualization. The sensory-motor physiology of the day and its application to willing and thinking as inhibited action provide reasonably certain connections between Phineas Gage, David Ferrier, and Sigmund Freud.

In general, this is an excellent introduction to the neuroscience of attachment. Its writing style tends toward the heavily prosodic rather than the more dryly scientific (which has both pluses and minuses, depending on one's preference). There are also problems in terms of overstatement and oversimplification of a number of complex issues (see below), but in general this would make a good adjunctive undergraduate text or early graduate text for any course focusing on the affective neuroscience of attachment. For those who have already digested large portions of the neuroscientific literature (including the various chapters pertaining to these topical domains in Panksepp's summary textbook, Affective Neuroscience, or Allan Schore's encyclopedic summaries) much of this work will seem introductory, but for those coming from a psychoanalytic (or neuroscience) background who have not been exposed to a great deal of this material, this text gives us a passionate reading on the nature of our most basic passions and our most irreplaceable needs and wishes. The book presents a compelling image of attachment as a biological mandate for all social and mammalian brains, essential to the regulation of our biology and homeostasis.

There are certainly issues one could raise about various aspects of the argument (see below for details), and some readers will find the prose a bit overstated, overblown, or dramatic, but I suspect the authors are trying to drive home as powerfully as possible basic points that neither many in neuroscience nor large segments of our affectively blinded culture adequately appreciate. From this standpoint, the book constitutes a valuable tonic to a culture increasingly addicted to a wide variety of substitutes and anodynes for the often badly missing and quite irreplaceable gratifications of intimacy, empathy, and social connection. Additionally for many readers, an overly wet prosodic style might be considerably preferable to an overly dry one. The book makes a compelling argument that our brains cannot tolerate the absence of nurturance and the basic comforts of empathic connection in infancy, childhood, or adulthood, although there clearly is a gradient of broadly differential vulnerability as we move through stages of the lifecycle, with an increasing capacity to cope adaptively with aloneness and loss, if childhood foundations are solid.

Commentary on “Freud's Theory of Mind and Functional Imaging Experiments”

Howard Shevrin PHD

Howard Shevrin

Professor of Psychology, University of Michigan Medical Center
Ann Arbor, Michigan, U.S.A.

Howard Shevrin  

I have argued elsewhere (Shevrin, 2000) that contemporary cognitive psychology and cognitive neuroscience are highly effective in generating findings but woefully weak in generating theories to explain these findings or to predict yet-to-be-discovered phenomena, the ultimate test of a good theory. Now Shulman and Reiser raise serious questions about the methods themselves underlying the generation of these findings.

They question the modular approach of cognitive psychology on which imaging studies in cognitive neuroscience are based. They point out that imaging studies do not account for the 80% of brain activity subtracted away so that investigators can more easily isolate the absolute increment of neuronal activity related to the stimulus under study. They demonstrate that far from being absolute, this increment is in part a function of the total neuronal activity in the activated region. The so-called resting activity of the brain is not to be treated as “noise”—random neuronal events uncorrelated with the activation of interest that can simply be ignored. Quite to the contrary, Shulman and Reiser argue that this “resting” activity is the essence of the mind-brain subjectivity constantly interacting and affecting other activity. They emphasize that this activity is sensitive to context and individual factors. And lastly, but most importantly, one can begin to make sense of this “resting” activity if one assumes that a good deal of it is unconscious. The theory they draw upon to conceptualize the nature of this unconscious activity is Freud's topographical theory, the earliest of his efforts to conceptualize the relationship between conscious and unconscious processes, and one, interestingly, that has come under attack within psychoanalysis itself.

Using their critique of cognitive neuroscience methodology and new findings concerning the extent of the ignored background activity, Shulman and Reiser propose a two-phase approach for imaging studies. The first and vital step would be to treat background activity as an independent variable by manipulating its level. For example, background activity is much lower under anesthesia than in the waking state. It is also known that the nature of background activity changes qualitatively in different sleep stages. The second step would involve introducing some critical stimulus at these different levels of background activity, thus making it possible to investigate the interactions between levels of background activity and stimulus processing. Drawing upon the psychoanalytic theory of primaryprocess mentation, they hypothesize that to the extent that background activity is unconscious, primary-process mechanisms would prevail.

Claudio Colace   Public Sanitary Service, Service for Drug Addiction, ASL Viterbo, Civita Castellana, Italy.

The study of dreams in drug-addicted subjects who typically show an abnormal desire to use drugs (i.e., drug craving) represents a new clinical contribution to the investigation of the role of motivations in dreaming processes. This paper reports two studies on the dreaming of heroin-addicted patients. These studies show that: (a) patients frequently dream about heroin (“using heroin” or “seeking and attempting to use heroin”) during abstinence (i.e., drug-craving frustration); and (b) dreams about heroin occur only in abstinent subjects and not in those who regularly use heroin. These results are largely compatible with the previous literature on dreaming in other forms of addiction. Drug dreams undoubtedly show that a clear specific motivational state (drug craving) is strongly involved in the occurrence of dreams clearly related to it. The implications of these data for dream research and theory are discussed.

Martina Rowley  

This paper reports an empirical reinvestigation of data collected by Karen Kaplan-Solms and Mark Solms. It focuses on neurological patients with medial frontal lesions, who exhibit striking and strongly held false beliefs, generally referred to as confabulations. Most accounts of the cause of confabulations are cognitive, focusing on the importance of memory or executive deficits. This study attempts to test the underinvestigated suggestion that confabulations may not be emotionally neutral, having a (“wish-fulfillment”) bias that shapes the patient's perception of reality in a more affectively positive direction. When recast in psychoanalytic terms, this proposal is consistent with Kaplan-Solms and Solms's (2000) claim about the role of Freud's (1915) special characteristics of the system unconscious in understanding confabulation. The present study tests this claim by a quantitative investigation of the process notes from which the Kaplan-Solms and Solms account was generated. We replicated our previous claim that confabulations show a positive emotional bias, finding that the vast majority (79%) of confabulations occurred when the patients were in a low mood state and, simultaneously, when the confabulations were affectively positive. The possible importance of these findings, and a range of important methodological issues in relation to these data, are discussed.

The French group was founded in January 2000. Stora, the acting chairman of the group, runs a consultation office for psychosomatics. The group consists of clinical psychologists, psychoanalysts, medical doctors, and researchers in many different fields of medicine. The neuroscientific approach is a shared concern, and we are interested in trying to link psychological, neurological, and somatic processes to each other.

Smirnow writes from Washington D.C. about their four-year-old study group on “Brain Science and Psychoanalysis.” During the past year they have formed a joint group of the Washington Psychoanalytic and Baltimore-Washington Psychoanalytic Institutes. They have studied several authors who have written on the development of affective structures, including Panksepp, Schore, and Watt. Their discussions have led them to the question they plan to study during the 2004-2005 academic year: How does psychotherapy change the brain? They also hope to have some neuroscientists join the group.

The group in Vienna, under the leadership of Gyuri Fodor, is still meeting and trying to follow up on new developments. However, they are also finding it difficult to start the research projects they had hoped to embark on. From the Northwest Chapter of the Neuro-Psychoanalysis Society, in the United States, John Espy reports that they are continuing their monthly meetings through the summer months of 2004. After having discussed Freud's Interpretation of Dreams from a neuro-psychoanalytic perspective, they moved on to his Jokes and their Relation to the Unconscious. In an attempt to better promote neuro-psychoanalysis in the Northwest, they are also looking at the possibility of having a winter “meeting” locally, attracting people from the Seattle area for a day or so of good discussion.

When you receive this issue of the journal, pleasant memories from the Rome Congress will still linger, while we will be looking forward to the next meeting. In the meantime, don’t hesitate to contact me if you have anything to ask about setting up a study or research group. It does not have to be “advanced science”—and it requires only that you start out from where you are. I am looking forward to hearing from you.

Antonio Damasio's Looking for Spinoza

Jaak Panksepp and Douglas Watt

Douglas Watt

Douglas Watt   Director of Neuropsychology, Quincy Medical Center, Boston University School of Medicine, Quincy, Massachusetts, U.S.A.

We take this opportunity to share a few closing remarks regarding our review and Antonio Damasio's reply.1 First, we appreciate Damasio's commentary and feedback, and it was not totally unexpected that a fair amount of it would be critical. It is understandable that Damasio would like his body of work to be considered as a whole rather than on the basis of a single book. We would, of course, expect no less, even though our aim, as is appropriate in such a review, was to focus largely on what we perceived to be problematic messages in Damasio's most recent contribution (granted that both of us had written especially laudatory reviews of his second book, and this one did not really cover new ground but developed issues where we do have disagreements). We are glad that Damasio's clarified his position on many of the issues we raised, and in general we tend to agree with the majority of the elaborations he has provided, although we do very much regret that he experienced our position as involving any version of an indictment for his failing to adhere to what he seemed to consider our “ideological position.”

We are especially pleased that he has clarified his perspective on the issue of affective experience in other animals, for that, as he surely appreciates, continues to be a sticking-point in the study of animal mind, largely as a legacy of the behaviorist ontology. We still believe his “strategic solution” provides no obvious practical advantages compared to simply accepting affect or some version of a subjective feeling state to be an intrinsic property of emotional systems in action within an intact brain. Although conceptually his strategic position has some appeals as he outlines, we are still concerned that such an approach would all too easily serve to sustain an undesirable and dualistic-type split between the animal and human work. Damasio's thinking and scientific work, coming as it does from a clinical neurology tradition (similar to DW's), has not been impeded by the no-mind-please behaviorist tradition as much as the professional zeitgeist in JP's field, but if one appreciates the deep history of this troubled field (e.g., for a compelling portrayal, see Rollins, 1998), then it should be easier to understand our passionate concerns about Damasio's compromise to parse emotions and feelings in the behaviorism-compliant way that he did. However, that type of strategy reduces the likelihood that neuroscientists will openly talk about feelings of animals in ways that can be empirically studied (e.g., Knutson, Burgdorf, & Panksepp, 2002), and we believe that it is through the intensive utilization of relevant animal models that we will eventually obtain a robust causal understanding of the sources of human emotional feelings (albeit not our human cognitions and thoughts about our feelings).

Mark Blechner

Mark Blechner

Mark Blechner   Training and Supervising Analyst, William Alanson White Institute of Psychiatry, Psychoanalysis and Psychology, New York.

Pleasantness is Relative

Psychoanalysts are usually better at generating hypotheses about the behavior of their patients than at proving or disproving these hypotheses by empirical methods with suitable controls. We therefore welcome studies like that of Turnbull, Jenkins, and Rowley, which assess the hypotheses and impressions of psychoanalysts using more objective measures and controls. I am going to discuss their paper from two vantage points: (1)the findings of the study and how they might change using alternative methodologies; (2) the general questions raised by the paper concerning psychological patterns in confabulation and the specific characteristics of “The Unconscious.”

The study uses independent raters to assess the impressions of clinicians about their own patients. The authors take clinical data from Kaplan-Solms and Solms (2000), from which they select confabulatory material, which they then have assessed by independent raters for “pleasantness.” The hypothesis of the study seems to be that if motivational factors such as wish-fulfillment are involved in confabulation, the confabulations will tend to be more pleasant than unpleasant.
