Yoram Yovell MD PHD

Yoram Yovell

Head, Trauma Studies Program, Faculty of Social Welfare and Health Studies; University of Haifa
Mount Carmel, Israel.

Yoram Yovell  

During the last two decades, functional brain imaging has emerged at the forefront of the neuroscientific study of the interface between mind and brain. In their thoughtful and original paper “Freud's Theory of Mind and Functional Imaging Experiments,” Shulman and Reiser critique some of the implicit assumptions that have been made in designing functional imaging experiments of mental activity.

Specifically, they argue that Freud's topographical model (1900) could provide a conceptual framework of mental function that might account for the very high “baseline” metabolic activity of the brain. This activity is often subtracted out, and therefore ignored, in experiments that compare regional cerebral activity during the execution of a task, or during sensory stimulation, with “resting” brain activity. The authors propose that the “resting” activity—that is, the brain activity of the awake subject when she or he is not presented with any specific stimulus or task—is not background noise but rather “represents an aggregate of internal and subjective activities that must be accepted, for the present, as unexplained but measurable.” Despite its relevance, I am somewhat concerned that Drs. Shulman and Reiser's critique may have implicated the whole field of functional brain imaging in making naïve reductionistic assumptions about the negligibility of “baseline” cerebral activity. It is my impression that such assumptions are much less common today than they were perhaps a decade ago.

The authors' main argument is that even in regions that were found by the subtraction method to be specifically involved in a particular mental task, the high “baseline” activity implies that the brain devotes the overwhelming majority of its energy to support neuronal firing that is not narrowly related to that task, but is nevertheless crucial for its execution. Indeed, this “baseline” activity, which is usually subtracted out, is often 50 to 100 times greater than the remaining activation that is “specific” to the task. The authors base their argument on 13C MRS experiments with anesthetized rats that underwent forepaw stimulation. Although I am hard pressed to suggest how this might be done, one would like to see their argument supported by additional experiments in humans.

John DeLuca PHD

John DeLuca

John DeLuca   Professor of Physical Medicine & Rehabilitation, UMDNJ-New Jersey Medical School; Director of Neuroscience Research, Kessler Medical Rehabilitation Research and Education Corporation, West Orange, New Jersey, U.S.A.

Turnbull and coauthors begin with a definition of confabulation that is not universally accepted and is certainly not all-encompassing. They state that confabulation is “typically understood to represent instances of false beliefs: opinions about the world that are manifestly incorrect and yet are held by the patient to be true.” I must take issue with this circumscribed view of confabulation as simply “false beliefs.” In fact, confabulations are not always incorrect. Frequently, confabulations (especially following ventromesial frontal lesions) are actual memories (or actual events) that are temporally displaced, so that the actual item recalled may not be false. It is indeed true that patients will often vehemently defend their recollections as veridical. As such, it is not the “belief” that is false, but its accuracy (e.g., temporal context or intrusion of actual memories from different time periods such as past and present) that may be incorrect or “false” (see DeLuca, 2000a). Delusions are also false beliefs, but most confabulations from ventromesial frontal lesions are not delusions (DeLuca, 2000a).

Turnbull and coauthors provide several citations stating that the “emotion-based” account of confabulation may be central to the nature of confabulations provided. For instance, they quote Kinsbourne (2000) about the affective quality of the confabulation where patients “mostly confabulate about personal matters that are emotionally significant to them” (which as yet is not scientifically proven). They further state that in what appears to be a single case report (Fotopoulou, Solms, & Turnbull, 2004) 80% of the confabulations were of “positive affective transformations,” where the patient regularly described being engaged in business activities or “leisure” pursuits (are all business activities leisure?). This case was credited as being consistent with the work of Kaplan-Solms and Solms. However, the question must be asked, if in fact the content of confabulation consists of elements that are very common or frequent in a persons life (e.g., work, leisure), why must this be interpreted as somehow motivational, affectively driven, and be wish-fulfilling?

Concluding Remarks to the New York Meeting on the “Unconscious in Cognitive Neuroscience and Psychoanalysis”

Carlo Semenza MD

Carlo Semenza   Department of Psychology, University of Trieste, Italy.

A very important step forward has recently been taken in psychoanalysis by making a distinction between what remains unconscious because of the nature of the supporting memory system and those processes that have been made unconscious because of active repression. Significant progress can still be made following this line of investigation. However, most of the convenors at the New York conference on the unconscious have been interested in the neurological mechanisms underlying repression. Elucidating these mechanisms may encounter some difficulties, depending on which aspect is investigated of what may be a multifaceted, complex function. Recent findings in neuroscience reveal that the function of suppressing information is performed—even before learning itself—by a mainly subcortical circuit. The psychoanalytic mechanism of repression, however, insofar as it implies a change of meaning, must have cortical components whose neurological and cognitive aspects may be hard to investigate.

David Milrod's “The Concept of the Self and the Self Representation”

Arnold Goldberg MD

Arnold Goldberg

Arnold Goldberg   Cynthia Oudejans Harris MD Professor, Department of Psychiatry, Rush Medical College, Chicago, Illinois; Training and Supervising Analyst, Chicago Institute for Psychoanalysis, Chicago, Illinois, U.S.A.

Reading Dr. Milrod's paper1 is very much like reading a primer on psychoanalytic ego psychology written by someone who is a master of it and, so, able to make it sound clear and simple. Yet I could not help but feel that the author had somehow slept through the revolution. That revolution has occurred in the last twenty or thirty years in psychoanalysis and has made almost every sentence in Milrod's essay an issue either of argument or of downright error. Now some of these contentious points have to do with mere differences of viewpoint or even of vocabulary, as Milrod's notes in his mention of Stern and Kohut. That he chose not to pursue these intellectual paths is an option that I may believe is unfair to the reader, but it is one that can possibly be justified. However, some of his ideas about development are quite open to question, especially with present-day thought about nonlinear dynamic systems. I think the work of Thelen has forced us to give up on the linear model espoused by Milrod. And some of his ideas about infancy and infant development are clearly in error. The quaint story of the infant mind espoused by Anna Freud is really quite at odds with what one reads in human development journals. Here we enter an arena of error or misstatement that demands correction.

More to the point is Dr. Milrod's decision about just what comprises mainstream psychoanalysis (p. 16 fn.), and what he has decided to ignore. Most of his references are to the psychoanalysis of forty or fifty years ago, and yet most of the exciting work on the self has occurred in the last twenty years. If one couples this with the general philosophical outlook that Milrod's paper seems to support, the reader would hardly know of the current debate about the very uselessness of the concept of representationalism. Alas, this is more than unfair to the reader, since it threatens the entire basic enterprise under discussion by Milrod.

If one moves to the secondary point of the paper—the relationship between neuroscience and the self of psychoanalysis—there is no argument at all, since the issue is never really addressed in a substantive way. Owen Flanagan (2000) gives a nice example of a table seen both as a convenient place to place a dish and/or as a field in Hilbert space, composed mainly of empty space. We do not worry ourselves about the question of just how those moving electrons manage to get together to hold our lunch. These are two different perspectives, two separate universes of discourse, etc. etc. There is no gap between neuroscience and psychoanalysis. They are separate worlds. The self of Damasio should not be grafted onto that of Freud or anyone else. They derive from different data, and we must insist that the data of analysis can only yield a self that belongs to analysis. The present state of envy that some psychoanalysts seem to have for neuro- science is unfortunate, both to themselves and to our field. The present state of unwillingness to become acquainted with psychoanalysis outside the supposed mainstream of Dr. Milrod is more than unfortunate, since it serves to rigidify a field that should remain vital and open.

I struggled quite a bit with this review, as this book has much to recommend it and also some serious problems. The basic problem for me in a nutshell is that any serious student of neuroscience or psychoanalysis might readily offer that knocking down the notion of the mind as the Blank Slate is clearly knocking down a straw man. It is unlikely that anyone coming from a psychoanalytic background would think for a minute that human nature is any version of a Blank Slate. Additionally, anyone familiar with affective neuroscience would also be readily and obviously uncomfortable with any of the purported cultural assumptions that Dr. Pinker spends his entire book debunking. Additionally, although Pinker acknowledges that it is nature—nurture interactions that are deemed critical, the book seems determined to attack some version of a “nurture hegemony” that in my judgment is not nearly as rampant as Professor Pinker thinks.

So a real question might be, “Who in the psychological sciences, or among reasonably sophisticated laypeople, or anybody for that matter with basic emotional common sense, truly believes in the Blank Slate, and why does Dr. Pinker devote hundreds and hundreds of pages (in fact the book could have been put on a major diet) to this whole line of analysis?” One might take issue with Pinker's notion that some version of an assumption of a “Blank Slate” is the driving source for many modern problems and abuses. The heart of the question for me that I cannot quite answer is: “Why does Professor Pinker think that the rejection of any formal concept of human nature is such a rampant problem or ideology in the social, political, and psychological sciences?” Certainly, there are places where Dr. Pinker's analysis applies, but I'm hard-pressed to see such a blanket rejection of the concept of human nature as a widespread and terrible cultural cognitive distortion responsible for large amounts of human suffering. I would see a much more destructive and insidious set of distortions in our culture around the systematic denial and/or mystification of basic human emotional needs, and their substitution by a wide variety of addicting pursuits and seductive processes that our culture values and trumpets loudly. At least significant portions of the book seem to me tilting at windmills, and I see quite different political and social problems from the ones Pinker outlines. For example, one might emphasize the increasing gap between rich and poor nations, and between the rich and poor in our country, or the wholesale destruction of the environment and of irreplaceable ecosystems. Obviously these are just political opinions and not without some controversial aspects either, but one is left with the impression that in Pinker's mind these issues, if they appear in the analysis at all (which they do occasionally), appear secondary to various permutations on the notion that the mind is a Blank Slate. While there are certainly problems driven by denial of our nature (particularly our affective nature, which Pinker rarely focuses on), in my judgment they seem to pale next to other sources of human suffering. Pinker develops two corollary ideas that sit in his judgment close to this cultural nexus of destructive ideas—namely, the concept of “the noble savage” (that human beings are, in their “natural state,” good and peaceful and are only corrupted by societal influences and experience) and the second corollary concept of “the ghost in the machine” (that the immaterial soul is good and separate from the corruptible body).

A View from Contemporary Biology

Thomas Hoffman MD

Thomas Hoffman

Thomas Hoffman   Baltimore-Washington Institute For Psychoanalysis, Laurel, Maryland, U.S.A.

A rereading of Freud's Beyond the Pleasure Principle reveals remarkable echoes of language and conceptualization to modern cell biological principles. The similarities between the death instinct and apoptosis (programmed cell death) are noted in particular. An overview of apoptotic mechanisms in the cell is provided, including a description of genetic controls by genes homologous to those of lower organisms; a cascade of effector proteins (caspases); regulation by internal and external cellular signals; intracellular controls active in triggering, modulating, or promoting apoptotic activity; and the presence of pro-and anti-apoptotic genes. These examples enhance an understanding of the dichotomies, paradoxes, and dialectics that made the death instinct and related ideas so troublesome to subsequent authors in and outside psychoanalysis. Using a convergence of cell biology's views on cell death to update Freud's original understanding, one can better comprehend the coexistence of instincts and tendencies toward life and death, the advantages to the organism of establishing a steady state, and the potential consequences, mental and physical, of its perturbation. Examples from case studies and literature illustrate the usefulness of an approach guided by this synthesis.
